newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton prices fall in India, seen weak in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Cotton prices fall in India, seen weak in Pakistan.

text.p: Cotton prices fell in the week to Friday in India and Pakistan amid sluggish buying and higher supplies of fresh arrivals, dealers said.

Dealers in Karachi said prices slipped as supply of the new 1997/98 (July-June) crop increased while demand from spinners remained low. Prices could come off further in the next few sessions, they added.

"If spinners continue to buy small quantities, the rates are likely to fall further as the new-crop supply is on the rise," one dealer said adding spinners were well stocked and are buyers only at dips.
In the kerb market on Thursday, the NIAB-78 was quoted for 2,340/2,360 rupees per maund (37.32 kg) the K-68 for 2,550/2,570 and the MNH-93 for 2,550/2,565.
The market was closed on Friday because of a religious holiday. Trading will resume on Saturday, dealers said.
Following are the weekly cotton spot rates in rupees per maund issued by the private Karachi Cotton Association:

In India cotton prices suffered a setback on the domestic market in the week amid sluggish mill buying and the release of stocks by state-owned agencies after widespread rains in the producing centres, dealers said.

In spot deals Bengal-deshi fell by 45/50 rupees at 945/1,000 rupees per maund (37.32 kg) while Punjab saw-ginned slid by 10 rupees at 1,800/1,840 rupees per maund and F-414 slid by five rupees at 2,050/2,070 rupees per maund in the week.

Gujarat varieties too fell on higher selling. Wagad cotton fell by 300 rupees to 12,700 rupees per candy (355.56 kg kg) while Kala-ginned moved down by 200/300 rupees at 12,000 rupees per candy. Long-staple Gujarat Shankar-4 dropped by 400/500 rupees at 17,000/17,500 rupees per candy for the average variety and at 19,000/20,000 rupees for the superior variety.

"Supplies remained higher during the week as stockist and state-owned agencies remained active sellers following widespread rain in the producing centres as well as absence of fresh export quota by the Indian government," said Chandubhai Thakkar, a leading dealer.
"Unsold stock of cotton at present across the country is estimated at 2.40/2.50 million bales (170 kg each)," he said.
"It is too early to estimate for the new crop of the 1997/98 season but everybody in the market is optimistic about the new crop and overall sentiment remained subdued during the week," Thakkar said.
